body.text: On November 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) convicted Myanmar of genocide. As supporters of the Rohingya from Cox’s Bazar to The Hague wept and cheered with relief, legal experts were warning of a backlash against the world’s top court amid ramifications for Israel.

The British Institute of International and Comparative Law (BIICL) said some of the ICJ findings could be “particularly relevant to South Africa’s genocide case against Israel,” adding that “this judgment will have consequences far beyond Myanmar.”

That case – accusing Israel of committing genocide against the Palestinians in Gaza – is currently in the written pleadings stage, with a trial widely expected in 2029. The United Nations’ 1948 Genocide Convention lays out the definition of genocide as “acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.”

Israel rejects the genocide allegations, arguing its military campaign in Gaza targeted Hamas, not Palestinian civilians, and justified the carnage as self-defense in response to the October 7, 2023 attacks by Hamas. It has rebuked the ICJ’s rulings as distorted or biased.

Sonya Sceats, the BIICL’s chief executive officer, said a genocide committed by a state against its people – as Rohingya survivors testified – now has global consequences and the international courts deserve support.

“The tragedy of the backlash set to engulf the world’s top court after this ruling is that it has little to do with the Rohingya victims and survivors of genocide and everything to do with perceived implications for another brutal conflict thousands of miles away in the Middle East,” she said. “How states of all sizes respond to any politicized attacks on the court will be a test of their commitment to international justice not just for responding to atrocities but also more generally as an essential means of settling differences peacefully with equality of arms before an independent court.”

The ICJ heard that an estimated 10,000 Rohingya were killed in 2017 during what the Myanmar military described as a “clearance operations” and nearly 400 villages – about 40 percent of the almost 1,000 villages in three townships of northern Rakhine state – were partially or totally destroyed.

When reading the verdict, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said such clearance operations also involved the murder of infants, which “supports the inference that Myanmar’s security forces acted with the intent to prevent births among the group.”

“Bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance often followed the destruction… in turn, rapid construction took place on the cleared sites, including security installations, new villages and houses, and other civilian infrastructure,” he said.

Myanmar’s defense had argued that 10,000 people out of a Rohingya population of up to 1.4 million people did not constitute a genocide. About 1.2 million now reside in refugee camps like Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been reportedly killed in Gaza out of a total population of some 2.3 million people, counted before the Israeli invasion.
The ICJ also ordered a safe, voluntary and peaceful repatriation of the Rohingya to their homes in Myanmar while providing reparations and compensation where materially possible.

The ICJ can determine state responsibility but it lacks the ability to enforce its rulings against individuals like Min Aung Hlaing, who was commander-in-chief of Myanmar’s military during the 2017 genocide of the Rohingya and is now the country’s president. An arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing has been sought by prosecutors in the International Criminal Court (ICC), which does prosecute individuals. The ICC was criticized by U.S. President Donald Trump as a “rogue institution” during his September address in the U.N. General Assembly.

Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnes Callamard urged governments not to welcome Min Aung Hlaing on the international stage, adding the ICJ ruling was an historic and authoritative recognition of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya.

“The court’s clarification that genocidal intent can coexist with other goals, including military aims, is especially significant for other cases pending at the ICJ, such as the case brought by South Africa against Israel for alleged genocide against Palestinians in Gaza,” she said.
Sceats added the consequences for civilians in conflict zones are catastrophic. “International law is an essential safety net for us all and now is the moment to defend it,” she said.

“Promotion of peace was the guiding spirit behind the court when it was created after the horrors of the Second World War. Today that spirit needs urgent rekindling in the face of efforts to discredit and even dismantle international courts and increasing state resort to violence.”
